# Carrier review — Bexley Road, weeks two and three

2026-04-22, 09:15 to 10:35, in the terminal office with the yard screen up. Typed as we went, so quotes are close but not exact.

In the room: Terry Blake (terminal manager), Sunil Rao (yard systems), Wes Cardoza (me). On the phone: Marguerite Ilves (Portside), and Dwight Mensah of Crestline Haulage for the first half hour.

Sunil put the count up first. Three weeks of pilot, 31 appointments where nothing arrived at all. Two carriers account for 19 of them — Crestline 12, Vanguard 7. The other 12 are spread across nine carriers, one or two each, which Terry called noise and I'd agree with.

Dwight was straight about the Crestline 12. Their dispatch board doesn't carry our appointment time. Drivers get a "be there by" that comes off the customer's delivery window, and when the two disagree the driver follows the one his own dispatcher gave him. "You're not on my screen," he said. "The customer is on my screen." He offered to hand-copy the Bexley appointments into the board for the pilot, which he was clear is not something he can keep doing past it.

Then Terry stopped the meeting.

"Before we write another line about no-shows — who signs off on charging a carrier for a missed appointment? I asked it on the walkthrough in February. I asked it at the slot rules workshop. Iris put it on the steerco agenda in March and it came back the way it went in. Same question every time, and it has never once had an answer. I'm not writing another report until somebody tells me who reads it."

Nobody in the room could tell him. Iris wasn't on this one, and nobody from commercial has sat in a Dockside meeting since the March steerco, where they sent a delegate who took notes.

Marguerite, on the system half: Portside counts a no-show the moment the window closes with no gate scan against it, and that's the whole of what it does. There's no charge field, no rate, nowhere to hang one. A charge would be a contract action against the carrier agreement, raised by whoever administers those agreements, and she has never been told who that is at Meridian either. "We can hand you the number every Monday morning. What happens to it is not a Portside question."

Terry's line: the report has come to him three Mondays running and he has no authority to do anything with it. He didn't ask for it and doesn't want it.

The grace window is holding, which was the good news. Nobody has called to argue about the 30 minutes, not once in three weeks. Two trucks got worked in at 28 and 29 minutes past and both drivers thought that was normal.

One thing that came out of the count and is worth chasing: the report keys on the carrier code from the appointment, and Crestline books under three of them — Crestline Haulage, Crestline Logistics NE, and a broker code that resolves to the same dispatch office. On the report that reads as three carriers with four no-shows each rather than one with 12. Sunil says the codes are a yard system artifact going back to before he started and nobody has ever reconciled them.

Left open at the end:

- Sunil to map the carrier codes onto real operating companies before the next count
- Dwight to hand-copy Bexley appointments into the Crestline board for the rest of the pilot only
- the charge question, again, with nobody's name against it
